name: Dan Farrelly
bio: Dan Farrelly is CTO and co-founder of Inngest, a platform for durable serverless functions, workflows and agent orchestration. He was previously CTO at Buffer and created developer tools including Timezone.io and MailDev.

talks.title: Your agent architecture has a half-life of 6 months

sessions.scheduled_title: Your agent architecture has a half-life of 6 months

quotes.quote: So speaking of building agents if you've been building agents for more than 6 months, you've likely rewritten something, maybe more than once.
Some parts of your code likely survives. But did they survive by accident?
So, in my opinion, there are three discrete layers. First, the execution layer. I think of this as the brain. It's where flow, state, durability, retries happen.
This is models, prompts, tools, memory. This is the layer that changes the most.
So, prompts last weeks, if you're lucky, maybe maybe a single week. Uh the models that you use, months, again, if you're lucky. Uh but I think that execution can last years, if you do it right.
And what happens then is that one layer's half-life kind of leaks and drags the other components down. You're building it's technical debt by another name.
So, my thesis is think in layers. Decouple them. So, let's talk about what I mean.
But I think in a lot of these situations, the abstractions either are not there at all or they're too high-level or the layers merge.
And I define it as the execution layer as being the system responsible for running your code reliably, managing how, when, or whether each piece of work completes.
You can swap the model, swap the context, swap the sandbox, the execution layer should be able to remain the same.
So, for this this to work, a 3-hour run cannot hold state in memory or in disk. The state must live outside of the work.
So, if you can't see the entirety of a trace from the trigger through the whole stack, it's really hard to debug it, let alone improve your agent and keep evolving it.
So, using it for durability, snapshots, or something in state, I think is an anti-pattern.
So, I think of the sandbox as the hands and execution as the brain.
They're all long-running. They're asynchronous. They're delegated. That means that you need to be able to observe them all uh down to the core.
It's going to have maybe hundreds of calls to you know, maybe 200 tool calls. You're going to probably guarantee to have at least one failure in that.
So, the frameworks of 3 months ago were not designed to handle this. Right? Like you're going to need to design these systems yourself.
the middle of the execution layer, when your agent is running, is a key place to instrument and score your agents
Instead of a thumbs up, thumbs down, it's like did we open the PR, right? If it's a research agent, was this research saved? Was it a good report?
And I think if you can get your execution layer right and think about the right primitives, everything else can quickly evolve around it.

positions.claim: Prompts have a useful lifetime of weeks, models of months, but a well-designed execution layer can last years.
Most teams couple their execution, context, and compute layers together, which causes the shortest-lived layer to force rewrites of the others.
The execution layer is the stable layer worth investing engineering effort in, and getting it right prevents rewriting large components every six months.
A correctly architected system lets you swap the model, context, or sandbox without changing the execution layer.
A three-hour agent run cannot keep its state in memory or on disk; state must be durable and external to the work.
Manual checkpointing and log-based state rehydration are inadequate because those abstractions leak into other layers of the harness.
Without flexible orchestration primitives, harness logic ends up absorbing queues, workers, polling, backoff, and scheduling, producing bad abstractions.
Observability must span the full session trace including database errors, permissions issues, triggers, and performance — not just LLM and tool calls.
Using a sandbox for durability, snapshots, or state is an anti-pattern because sandboxes are ephemeral and stateless by design.
A background agent making on the order of 200 tool calls will almost certainly experience at least one failure.
Agent execution traces need to be inspectable by agents, not only by humans, so that reviewer functions can evaluate what was executed.
Frameworks from three months ago were not designed for loop and background-agent architectures, so teams must design these systems themselves.
The execution layer is the ideal hub for observability and agent scoring because user input, feedback, actions, and session results all flow through it.
Outcome-based signals such as whether a PR was opened or a report was saved are better evaluation data than thumbs up/thumbs down feedback.
A useful self-improving agent loop can be built from as few as three functions: a scheduled health check, a triage agent, and a periodic reviewer.
